articles.title_orig: Damage assessments, cleanup begin after Hurricane Isaias thrashes Florida Panhandle
articles.title_zh: Damage assessments, cleanup begin after Hurricane Isaias thrashes Florida Panhandle
articles.content_orig:
Isaias is now well inland over the Southeast but still has a threat of flooding rain, strong wind gusts and tornadoes in parts of the South and East through Sunday.
(MORE: Isaias maps tracker | live updates )
Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday night in the Florida Panhandle at Category 2 strength.
Wind gusts over 110 mph were clocked in several panhandle locations, along with storm surge flooding. Over 700,000 customers are without power in its wake.
We have a full recap of the events leading up to landfall at the bottom of this article.
Isaias is now "post tropical," which just means that it has lost its tropical characteristics, but there is still heavy rain and gusty winds with its inland remnants.
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
You can see where the rain is currently in the map below, along with any flash flood or tornado watches and warnings.
( MORE: What all these tropical terms mean )
The biggest threat left from Isaias this weekend is a threat of flash flooding, particularly in parts of the Southeast Saturday.
The heaviest additional rain is expected through Saturday night in the foothills of the Appalachians from eastern and northern Georgia to upstate South Carolina, western North Carolina and western Virginia.
It's there where the flash flood threat is highest, especially in hilly or mountainous terrain.
Other areas of heavy rain that could lead to flash flooding include:
Wind gusts capable of at least some tree damage and additional power outages will continue through early Sunday in parts of the Southeast, particularly where high wind warnings are in effect, shown on the map below.
Some gusts in the Smoky Mountains could reach 60 to 70 mph.
Trees could also be toppled more easily in ground soaked by heavy rain.
There is a threat for severe thunderstorms and tornadoes across Georgia, the eastern Florida Panhandle and into the Carolinas Saturday and Saturday evening.
This is common with the remnants of former tropical storms and hurricanes.
That threat of isolated tornadoes and strong thunderstorm wind gusts continues Sunday in the East.
Be prepared for power outages across the Southeast that could last at least several hours or possibly multiple days in areas that were under hurricane warnings near the Gulf Coast.
Avoid flood-prone areas and never drive into flooded stretches of roads.
Stay out of areas near the Gulf Coast impacted by the hurricane until local officials give the all clear to return.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, Friday evening with sustained winds of 105 mph, a Category 2 hurricane.
The highest gust recorded was 116 mph in Santa Rosa Sound, Florida, where sustained winds of 91 mph were also measured.
Pensacola reported a 102-mph wind gust earlier Friday evening. Gulf Breeze, Florida, located across Pensacola Bay from Pensacola, reported a wind gust of 97 mph and sustained winds of 83 mph.
Isaias ( ees-ah-EE-ahs) is one of the trickier names to pronounce on this year's list. To hear the correct pronunciation, listen here .
Isaias replaced "Ike" on one of the Atlantic name lists after that name was retired following the destructive, deadly 2008 hurricane .
It wasn't used during its first year of eligibility in 2014, since we only reached the eighth name, Hanna, that year.
However, the name was used in 2020 for a storm that eventually tracked up the East Coast with destructive winds.
Around 11 a.m. CDT Friday, an instrumented NOAA Saildrone measured a gust of 104 mph near the eyewall of Isaias, according to the National Hurricane Center.
In Venice, Louisiana, Plaquemines Parish local emergency management reported a gust of 53 mph.
An extreme wind warning was issued Friday evening for the western Florida Panhandle, including Pensacola and Destin, for the likelihood of wind gusts over 115 mph, but it has since expired.
Early observations show water levels surpassed 4.0 feet above normally dry ground in Destin and 5.6 feet in Panama City, Florida, and were likely higher in the western Panhandle.
One caveat with these storm surge totals is they are measured relative to the Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) and this number includes tide influences so they should not be interpreted as storm surge heights alone.
The highest wind gust reported was an impressive 117 mph three miles east-southeast of Oriole Beach. Two miles west southwest of Pensacola, at City Hall, a gust of 102 was reported.
There was a roof blown off the Rest and Relax Inn on Plantation Road in Pensacola. Multiple collapsed gas station canopies were reported in Pensacola (Blue Angel Parkway and Mobile Highway) and also in Crestview. Trees were uprooted, one of which crushed a business on Fort Walton Beach. There were also multiple RVs blown over, including one onto US 98 between Gulf Breeze and Navarre.
In Alabama, a gust of 75 mph was reported near Orange Beach while Birmingham saw a gust of 49 mph.
Trees fell directly onto residences in Mountain Brook, Birmingham (Five Points & Ensley), Opelika (manufactured home), and Ladonia (tree through a house).
All roads were impassable in Conecuh County due to debris and fallen trees.
Georgia saw a 68 mph gust in Warner Robins while Hartsfield-Jackson Airport saw a gust to 45 mph.
There were road closures due to downed trees across all lanes of State Route 91 near Stocks and on State Route 93 near Pelham and Spence.
In terms of heavy rainfall, Bellwood, Alabama, saw over a foot of rain in just 13 hours. Caney Creek/FAWN Station, Florida, saw 12.06 inches in 24 hours, with 9.67 falling in 3 hours and 4.15 inches falling in 1 hour.
Flash flooding reports were observed at Westland Apartments in Bellair, Florida, while flash flooding stranded a vehicle in floodwaters near Sale City, Georgia.
In Florida, Bayside Subdivision and Destin saw 7.18 inches and 7.52 inches of rainfall, respectively. The Greater Atlanta area saw 1-3 inches of rainfall in a 6 hour period early Saturday.
A flash flood warning was even in effect for part of Atlanta that morning.

articles.title_orig: Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia
articles.title_zh: Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia
articles.content_orig:
US president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end war
Donald Trump has said Ukraine needs “a new leader”, a day after making a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel.
The US president suggested Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war with Russia and blamed him for high diesel prices in the US.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
Trump made the comments as Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine , which Zelenskyy said were a “thanks” to Trump for the diesel deal.
The Ukrainian president has expressed outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November’s midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue.
The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.
He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.
That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 20 people, including three children.
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.
“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.
There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.
Andy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks.
The prime minister said he recognised the past day had been “difficult for Ukraine” and the two talked about the importance of keeping up pressure on Russia, No 10 said.
In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting ​an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.
“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” ​ Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.
The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.
Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.
The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.
Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said ​on Saturday.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.
Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The Financial Times reported that during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Rachel is behaving in unusual ways. What that means for SoCal this weekend
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Rachel is behaving in unusual ways. What that means for SoCal this weekend
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Tropical Storm Rachel brings with it  a slew of potential hazards, including damaging coastal flooding.
The National Hurricane Center warned that Rachel could pick up some strength before arriving on the West Coast — an unusual occurrence for storms in the tropical eastern Pacific.
Typically, storms weaken significantly once they enter those cooler waters. But El Niño conditions and an ongoing marine heat wave have pushed ocean temperatures 10 to 13 degrees higher than normal, providing a far-more-conducive environment for Rachel.
“It’s notable that this is an unusual event that’s being made possible by both coincidence of this early arriving low-pressure trough off the coast of California and the record warm — and I do mean record warm — ocean temperatures off the coast of California right now,” UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said during a briefing  Friday.
Rachel is expected to make landfall either in northern Baja California or San Diego County as early as Saturday night.
In the modern record, only two storms  have passed through the state at tropical-storm strength.
The first — nicknamed El Cordonazo, or the Lash of St. Francis — hit Long Beach and San Pedro in September 1939 . It dumped 5.62 inches of rain on L.A. over three days, spawned wind gusts of up to 65 mph and resulted in 45 deaths from flooding, with an additional 48 deaths at sea.
There was also Nora in September 1997, which was briefly at tropical storm strength as its center passed along the California-Arizona border, but California was spared the kind of damage it delivered to Baja California. Street flooding was reported in Imperial County, the Coachella Valley and San Diego, while big waves boosted by Nora and another storm sent breakers crashing into beachfront properties in Seal Beach, seriously damaging three homes and resulting in minor damage to 45 others.
The blistering heat that has baked Southern California for days is coming to an end, with rain on tap for the weekend and early next week, along with a risk of potentially damaging coastal flooding.
The National Weather Service office in San Diego on Friday issued a rare tropical storm watch for most of San Diego County, including San Diego, Chula Vista, Carlsbad and Oceanside, meaning that tropical storm-force winds are possible over the next 48 hours. It’s only the second time a tropical storm watch has  been issued in California.
Coastal flooding will remain the biggest concern for the region in the coming days, particularly for south-facing shores, given the combination of high tides, a higher-than-typical water level and the arriving tropical storm. Swells will not only bring the potential for water intrusion, but also hazardous surf — ranging from 3 to 6 feet in some areas — and rip currents, according to the weather service.
Officials had predicted that tides in Southern California would be 1 foot to 1.5 feet above normal what would ordinarily be expected without the abnormally warm ocean temperatures wrought by El Niño .
Around 9 a.m. Friday, the high tide in San Diego and La Jolla was coming in 17 inches higher than the official prediction, which doesn’t account for hotter-than-normal ocean waters or swells from tropical storms, according to NOAA’s tide forecasts. Tides were coming in 16 inches higher than the official prediction in Santa Monica and 14 inches higher in San Francisco as of Friday morning.
“We’ve got water that’s already high and then we’re going to have periods of high tides each morning and evening and then on top of that we have high surf,” said Miguel Miller, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in San Diego. “We have all these things stacking up on each other and we’ve already seen in recent weeks how just the high tides, even without the large surf, is putting water into places where it doesn’t usually go.”
Forecasters are warning that south-facing beaches in Southern California could be particularly at risk of flooding on account of Tropical Storm Rachel this weekend.
A coastal flood advisory for Ventura, Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego counties — warning of the potential for flooding in beach parking lots, boardwalks and roads, with isolated road closures expected, along with minor coastal erosion — is expected to remain in effect through Tuesday afternoon.
Coastal cities including Laguna Beach, Newport Beach and Long Beach have already seen significant flooding. Long Beach issued a mandatory evacuation order for residents of Seaside Walk between 64th and 66th Place.
While tropical moisture from the remnants of Rachel is expected to deliver only light rain to much of Southern California between Sunday morning and Monday night, the Mojave Desert, the Inland Empire and portions of San Diego County could see more significant precipitation.
The weather service is warning that there is a moderate, or 40% chance, of excessive rainfall that could lead to flash flooding in places like San Diego, El Cajon, Chula Vista, Escondido, Palm Springs and Twentynine Palms. A moderate risk means that numerous flash floods are likely, and that many streams may flood. There is a chance that the San Diego River near Fashion Valley could reach minor flood stage.
There’s also a 15% chance of that occurring in Oceanside, San Clemente, Laguna Niguel, Riverside, San Bernardino, Las Vegas and the California-Arizona border; and a 5% chance in places like Huntington Beach, Santa Ana, Long Beach, Anaheim, Pomona, Victorville, Barstow, and most of Arizona and southern Utah.
Newport Beach was one of several coastal communities to see flooding Friday as residents braced for Tropical Storm Rachel, which is expected to cause more issues over the weekend.
In Los Angeles County, rain is expected to be light to moderate, ranging from about a quarter of an inch to an inch across much of the region. A bit more rain is expected in the San Gabriel Mountains, according to the weather service office in Oxnard. Rain rates are probably going to be a quarter of an inch per hour or less, making debris flow and landslides unlikely.
A bit more rain is expected in Orange County with coastal areas receiving from half an inch to an inch over the weekend and into early next week. Coastal sections of San Diego County could see between an inch and an inch and a half of precipitation with higher rain levels predicted farther inland.
Nora arrived during a “very strong” El Niño season. That pattern is linked to above-average hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific, and also is usually tied to above-average rainfall for Southern California in the winter.
That climate pattern sees the heating of ocean waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, which spur changes in the atmosphere that can affect weather around the world.
Strong surf across Southern California this weekend blasted through a seawall in Long Beach, caused a massive sinkhole at a celebrity’s Malibu home and damaged several Dana Point homes, among other issues.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center said  Thursday that there is virtually a 100% chance that the El Niño this season will be categorized as “very strong.” There’s also an 83% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest on record, which goes back to 1950, up from a 75% probability forecast last month.
“With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed,” the Climate Prediction Center said Thursday.
There have been only four “very strong” El Niños in the modern record — 1982-83, 1991-92, 1997-98 and 2015-16. Two of them — in 1982-83 and 1997-98 — deluged downtown Los Angeles with more than 30 inches of rain, more than double the area’s average annual rainfall.

China and the European Union have the potential to deepen economic and trade cooperation by addressing their differences through negotiations and providing businesses with a more stable and predictable environment, a Chinese trade expert told CGTN on Saturday, following the two sides' latest trade talks in Beijing.
The remarks followed the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, co-chaired by Chinese Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic in Beijing from Thursday to Friday. A joint statement released on Friday said the two sides had agreed to maintain stable bilateral economic and trade ties and make them more balanced.
"The statement has made it very clear that both sides agree that we are going to negotiate in a better way," said Zhou Mi, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.
China and the EU have complementary advantages in markets, innovation and businesses, Zhou said, adding that the two sides could better address uncertainties and restrictions through dialogue.
He said policy stability and predictability were crucial to encouraging businesses to invest and expand cooperation. "When enterprises are going to make investments, they have to understand that the situation will be stable."
Supply chains and industrial chains are built on collaboration and trust, Zhou said, adding that businesses would be more willing to strengthen ties if they believed cooperation would bring them further opportunities.
The joint statement outlined 16 areas of consensus, covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform. The two sides also agreed to continue exploring the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain goods within the framework of WTO rules and reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles.
Zhou said China and the EU could help restore confidence in global trade governance amid growing uncertainty and protectionism.
China and the EU are firm supporters of globalization, he said, calling for stronger support for the multilateral trading system, including through improvements to dispute settlement and efforts to address emerging issues such as e-commerce.
The two sides also identified potential cooperation in artificial intelligence, the digital economy and new energy. Zhou said turning that potential into concrete business and investment opportunities would depend partly on whether companies had confidence in policy stability and the prospects for cooperation.
China and the EU agreed to hold their next meeting under the trade and investment consultation mechanism in March 2027, with a ministerial video conference scheduled for January. Both sides also agreed to maintain close communication and promote the early implementation of the agreed outcomes.

articles.title_orig: Will We Ever Understand Dementia?
articles.title_zh: Will We Ever Understand Dementia?
articles.content_orig:

At 9.30am on June 16, 2022, Megan* braced herself and clicked on the Zoom link. She was about to find out whether she had the gene mutation for early onset Alzheimer’s disease . She knew the condition was in her family; she’d watched her own mother – a woman who loved to cook and dance, who changed her curtains to match the seasons – die at 65, after almost 15 awful years. “She was a husk,” says Megan. “She couldn’t speak, she weighed 40 kilograms.” Two uncles and an aunt had also died of Alzheimer’s, and her maternal grandmother. There was a 50/50 chance she had the mutation – and if she did, there was a 100 per cent chance she’d get the disease.
Megan was 55 years old at the time, with thick hair, blue eyes and unlined skin. Trained as a nurse, she was married, with three sons and an air of practical kindness: the sort of person who stops at the zebra crossing even if the pedestrian isn’t quite there yet; who says hello to everyone she sees on the street in her small home town in rural Victoria. She had no symptoms of cognitive decline, no signs of trouble at all. But a determinative mutation is like a time bomb. It will go off – the only question is when.
The genetic counsellor joined the Zoom call. At 9.35, she broke the news. Megan has the same mutation as her mother – a pathogenic variation to her Presenilin 1 gene (PSEN1). She will get Alzheimer’s disease.
Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, accounting for up to 70 per cent of cases worldwide. The rest is split between frontotemporal lobe dementia, Lewy body dementia, vascular and mixed dementias, Huntington’s and Parkinson’s disease dementia, and various dementias caused by brain injury. There are even, rarely and tragically, more than 100 genetic conditions that cause dementia in children.
Like every other form of dementia, Alzheimer’s is caused by the progressive death – often over years – of tens of billions of brain cells (at autopsy, the brain of someone with dementia may have a volume of up to 40 per cent less than that of a healthy person). It was first described in 1901, when Alois Alzheimer, a notably dedicated and meticulous German physician, took a 51-year-old woman called Auguste Deter, a seamstress, wife and mother, into his care. Alzheimer gave Deter some simple tests, including writing her own name. “Auguse”, she wrote, her pen trailing away on the “e”. “I have lost myself, so to speak,” she told him.
Over the following years, Alzheimer could do nothing to help as Deter’s condition deteriorated. But he continued caring for her for free, and when she died in 1906 he conducted her autopsy, preparing the first microscope slides ever to reveal the two “peculiar substance[s]” now known to be the twin hallmarks of Alzheimer’s: amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles.
After Megan heard the news that winter morning, she got off Zoom, left her house, and started walking. After a few minutes, a car pulled up beside her. It was her sister, Jillian, who lives in the same town, on her way home from work. Jillian was also 55 years old, with thick hair, blue eyes and unlined skin. Also a trained nurse, also a mother to three children, she is six minutes younger than Megan, and her identical twin.
Jillian leaned over, and Megan bent down to the window. “I took one look at her face,” says Jillian now, “and I knew. I went home and said to my husband, ‘I’ve got it. I’ve got it too.’ ”
Why does dementia have such a grip on the human imagination? In surveys around the world, people – especially as they reach mid-life – routinely name it as their greatest health fear: greater than heart disease, greater even than cancer. Perhaps it’s because it feels so close: as simple as blanking on a word, misplacing the remote, getting lost in a sentence – and also so inconceivably far away. In what unimaginable world could we end up oblivious to the things we love, not knowing our own names, no longer recognising the faces of our children? Dementia, above all, is a disease of loss: how could we bear to know such losses are coming?
This is exactly what Megan and Jillian are facing. Jillian’s own genetic counselling appointment was at noon on the same day as her sister’s. At 12.01, she confirmed she, too, had the PSEN1 mutation. Alzheimer’s was coming for her, too.
The next few months were horrendous for both women. “I started walking in the dark,” says Megan. “Walking down dark laneways, hoping I would come across someone in a bad mood.” “And I just cried,” says Jillian. “Shane [her husband] and I just cried and cried for weeks.”
Things are much better now – of which more later – but, as Jillian puts it, they’re always wondering if this might be the day Alzheimer’s symptoms begin. “You forget to do something, you do something stupid, and you go, ‘Is this it?’ ” she says. “I’ll say to Shane, ‘Is that it starting already?’ ”
No wonder she’s worried. Last year, for the first time ever, dementia became the biggest cause of death in Australia: a 39 per cent rise in the past decade alone. Ninety thousand new dementia cases are now being diagnosed each year, and one in 12 Australians are either living with it, or looking after someone who is. As other fatal diseases – cancer, heart disease – have become increasingly treatable, dementia has not. Despite millions of research hours and billions of research dollars, there is still no cure. Just as it was 120 years go, dementia today is a death sentence.
But now, finally, things are changing. In the past 12 months, two breakthrough new drugs have been approved, a new diagnostic blood test has become available, and new research about prevention and rehabilitation has been published. And so, for the first time in history, we can legitimately ask: can the future of dementia be different from the past?
We’ve known for more than a generation that most dementia is caused by the mis-formation of proteins in the brain. These proteins – different in different forms of dementia – are all present in healthy brains, but in dementia they go rogue, destroying neuronal function. This process can begin years – even decades – before symptoms are evident. But eventually, as it progresses, the most fundamental processes of life – heartbeat, breathing, swallowing – are compromised. Most people with dementia die of aspiration pneumonia, when food is accidentally sucked into the lungs.
What we haven’t known until recently, however, is that almost half of all cases are preventable – or at least delayable. Contrary to popular myth, less than one per cent of all dementia is inevitable, caused by determinative – 100 per cent guaranteed – gene variants like Megan’s and Jillian’s. Even “risk” genes, like the APOE4 gene variant Chris Hemsworth carries , only increase your susceptibility; they don’t cause disease outright. So for many of us, dementia is, to a greater or lesser extent, avoidable. And in July, the World Health Organisation updated its official dementia guidelines to reflect this fact, stating that “up to 45 per cent of the risks can be attributed to modifiable risk factors such as tobacco, alcohol use, social isolation, physical inactivity, air pollution and noncommunicable diseases, including high blood pressure and diabetes.”
Many healthy people do get dementia; many risks are beyond our control. But if possible, why not try to modify the ones we can?
Kaarin Anstey is the director of the UNSW Ageing Futures Institute. She studies non-pharmacological interventions for dementia. Drilling down on the WHO risk factors, she explains that type 2 diabetes “increases the risk of dementia by about 72 per cent for men. In women, it’s 77 per cent. Traumatic brain injury doubles the risk for men, and increases it by about 50 per cent for women. Untreated depression is an 82 per cent increased ri

articles.title_orig: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
articles.title_zh: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
articles.content_orig:
As the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft , claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas.
The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers.
Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended.
The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad.
All eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45.
Amazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals.
The numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.

articles.title_orig: Palestinian Authority president postpones legislative elections another year, marking 20 years without a vote
articles.title_zh: Palestinian Authority president postpones legislative elections another year, marking 20 years without a vote
articles.content_orig:
President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.
Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority's credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas' party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas' presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.
The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.
Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas' Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.
The West Bank has grown increasingly violent in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority's control are both regularly reported.
Though the U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year outlined a future role for the authority, its immediate role was left mostly undefined as Hamas has continued to govern and the technocrats under the Board of Peace remain in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza to transition power.
Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election. But behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan. Dahlan had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas and was exiled in 2010 after a falling-out with Abbas.
"Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.

articles.title_orig: ‘Ship has sailed’: New poll shows even an end to the war or lower gas prices may not save Republicans
articles.title_zh: ‘Ship has sailed’: New poll shows even an end to the war or lower gas prices may not save Republicans
articles.content_orig:
President Trump delivers remarks in Clarksville, Tennessee.
by CORY SMITH | The National News Desk
(TNND) — Republicans may be running out of time to improve voters' outlook on the economy before the midterms, with new surveys showing widespread pessimism, price concerns, and blame for President Donald Trump's policies.
“We're less than four weeks away from the election, and you can't do any sort of economic policy that's going to work that quickly,” said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University. “It just doesn't happen that way.”
The University of Michigan’s index of consumer sentiment ticked down just a bit in a preliminary October reading released Friday , coming off a four-month low in September .
October’s final reading of consumer sentiment from the University of Michigan will be released Oct. 23, but the month is on pace for a 13.6% yearly decline.
Meanwhile, the Pew Research Center released results Thursday from a survey conducted Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, which found more Americans rate national economic conditions as poor (42%) than excellent or good (21%). Another 37% rate conditions as only fair.
Democratic views of the economy have been consistently negative since Trump returned to office, but the Pew Research Center has also recorded a slide in sentiment this year among Republicans. In January, 49% of Republicans rated economic conditions as good or excellent. Now, just 36% do.
The new Pew Research Center survey found most Americans, 65%, view Trump’s policies as having made the economy worse.
Once again, Democrats have consistently seen Trump’s economic policies in a negative light. And once again, Republican support for Trump’s policies has started to slide.
In January, 57% of Republicans said Trump’s policies made economic conditions better. Now, just 39% of Republicans say the same.
Most Americans said in the Pew Research Center survey that they’re very concerned about the cost of food, health care and housing.
Close to three-quarters of Americans, including 65% of Republicans, said they were very concerned about gas and energy prices.
Only 26% of Americans said they expect economic conditions to be better a year from now.
“Well, it's true that the polls, which have gotten the president's success wrong every time, have been saying that people are looking a little bit depressed about the economy,” White House Economic Adviser Kevin Hassett told CNN in a recent interview . “But if you look at their actions, the actions speak way louder than words.”
Hassett, who criticized consumer sentiment polls as over-indexing the views of Democrats, pointed to Americans’ robust spending habits in saying that folks are “really optimistic about the future.”
Indeed, holiday shopping forecasts have pointed to a bright season for retailers, despite gloomy consumer sentiment. Mastercard, for example, projected holiday spending growth of 5.5%.
“Just because people are planning to spend for the holidays doesn't mean that they're not unhappy about it,” Belt said.
Belt said economic concerns are likely to be the top motivating factor for voters in next month’s election, which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.
“Always are, and this year it will be even more so,” he said.
The Pew Research Center found that the economy ranks as the top voting issue this year, over issues such as the future of democracy, education, immigration, foreign policy and crime.
The Pew Research Center also said Trump’s approval rating now stands at a second-term low of 30%. And its survey shows Democratic voters are more motivated than GOP voters heading into the midterms.
Political prognosticators generally expect Democrats to gain enough seats to flip the House. The Senate is more up in the air, but Belt said the eroding consumer sentiment has the Senate also looking more likely to fall to Democrats.
“I think it's really instructive that we're really seeing a decline among Republicans, as well, on their attitudes about the economy. ... It's not just the independents. It's not just Democrats being Democrats because there's a Republican in office,” Belt said. “This is something that's affecting everybody, and they're really concerned about it.”
Joanne Hsu, the director and chief economist of the University of Michigan consumer survey, told The National News Desk a couple of weeks ago that sentiment has taken a “pretty substantial slide” since the start of the year, driven lower by concerns over higher gas prices that people fear will reverberate through the wider economy.
And she noted that the cost-of-living concerns are being expressed by people across the political spectrum.
FILE - A person pumps gas at a Mobil gas station on June 25, 2026, in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
Ted Rossman, the principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, said there’s somewhat of a disconnect between the economic mood in the country and the economy's actual performance.
The so-called K-shaped economy helps explain part of that, he said. Higher-income Americans have benefited from rising home and stock values, and their spending is helping to prop up the economy.
Rossman said a relatively low unemployment rate has also supported spending.
But Americans also feel as though their wage gains are being gobbled up by higher costs.
And Rossman said debt is fueling a lot of Americans’ spending.
MMI, the nonprofit consumer debt and credit counseling agency Rossman works for, has seen a 10-year high for enrollment in debt management plans and five straight years of growing demand for financial counseling.
“The mood continues to be very gloomy,” Rossman said. “As you know, a lot of the actual economic data – the harder numbers on jobs and spending and GDP growth and all that – those have been more positive. So, it does beg the question of what's going on. Some of it is that the relationship between sentiment and hard data has weakened. It used to be that sentiment was a predictor of the future, and if people were feeling bad about the economy, pretty soon they would start pulling back on spending. People have been warning about that for years, and it just hasn't happened.”

articles.title_orig: In three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield
articles.title_zh: In three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield
articles.content_orig:
A whirlpool of violence has engulfed everywhere from Lebanon to Yemen. Meanwhile, the west has destroyed any political authority it once had
T here was a world before 7 October, 2023, and now there is a world after. For Gaza, for Israel , for the wider Middle East, and for everyone else too. Not all hinge points in history are obvious at the time. Three years on from the day it began, and precisely one year since a supposed ceasefire was agreed, this one is now impossible to ignore.
The before-and-after pictures tell part of the story. An update to Google Maps, released last week , underscores just what three years of relentless Israeli military onslaught has done to Gaza. Satellite images show how entire towns have been reduced to rubble. Mosques and hospitals, visible three years ago, have now disappeared. Meanwhile the once-empty shoreline is now crammed with tents. This is what it looks like when an attempt has been made to destroy a people.
For Israel, too, there has been a before and after. Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had cultivated a sense of security, even of impregnability. The ease with which Hamas carried out its terrorist attack, killing 1,200 Israelis, including hundreds of young people at a music festival, destroyed that belief for ever.
Three years on from 7 October, both Israel and Gaza have changed beyond recognition. But the consequences of Hamas’s attack and Israel’s brutal response, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, have spread far wider.
Under the pretext of protecting its own borders, Israel has launched wars and military offensives across the region, sending troops into Syria; effectively annexing parts of southern Lebanon, deploying the same tactics there that it used in Gaza; and starting, with the US, an unwinnable war with Iran that has spiralled into a regional conflict affecting all six Gulf states.
The Iran war has sparked a new conflict between the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, which this week triggered a mutual defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey, dragging two other countries into the maelstrom. Across the Red Sea, some of the same combatants are involved in the war in Sudan and a fresh conflict inside Ethiopia .
More than a dozen countries across two continents are now entangled in a rising number of wars, with overlapping participants and numerous competing interests.
But there is something else, more insidious, that has changed. The rule of international law, tenuous as it was, has been openly replaced by military might. In 2022, western leaders – building a coalition rightly opposed to Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – made moral appeals based on the violation of international law. In Gaza, they encouraged and supported Israel, even when it was clear that the rules were being broken. That hypocrisy has not gone unnoticed, not just in the global south but among many millions of citizens in the west.
We have watched this happen in real time. Despite the ban on international journalists, anyone with a phone knew what was happening in Gaza from the early days of Israel’s response. Hundreds of Palestinian journalists have reported on the bombing of hospitals and schools, the bombing of cafes and wells, the killings at food distribution points, the deaths of children and babies. War crimes have never before been broadcast in real time, relentlessly, every hour of every day, around the world.
Gaza has also changed how wars are fought. Israel has pioneered the use of AI to select targets, accelerating our descent into a future for which we are unprepared.
A ll of this was allowed to take place in a time when the west could still argue that the “international rules-based order” existed. It may have been destroyed by Donald Trump, but we cannot forget that the dismantling began under Joe Biden. It was Biden who ensured the flow of weapons to Israel continued uninterrupted, Biden who insisted that every United Nations security council resolution calling for a ceasefire was vetoed , and Biden who attacked the international criminal court when it sought to indict Netanyahu for war crimes.
US support for Israel has always been strong and, on the whole, unquestioned. But even Republican presidents have understood they have influence over Israel’s actions and have been prepared to use it.
Ronald Reagan suspended an arms deal in 1981 after Israel annexed the Golan Heights. A year later, his administration stopped supplying cluster weapons to Israel after Menachem Begin’s government used them in populated areas during its invasion of Lebanon. In 2002, the killing of 15 Palestinians in Gaza was enough for Colin Powell, the then secretary of state, to announce a review of Israel’s use of American arms .
Israel was also given a free pass by every other member of the G7, including those run by centrists or centre-left politicians. French president Emmanuel Macron, German chancellor Olaf Scholz, Justin Trudeau in Canada and Australia’s Anthony Albanese all initially gave Israel their backing.
Only António Guterres, the much-maligned UN secretary general, emerges with a modicum of credit. Less than three weeks after 7 October, he called Israel’s response “collective punishment of the Palestinian people” and demanded an immediate ceasefire.
The one ray of hope for the future is that our shared understanding of what has happened over the past three years means that in many countries the political winds have shifted.
Before Andy Burnham even entered Number 10, he apologised for how Labour had handled the early days of the conflict. The UK now has a prime minister who was one of the few western politicians to call for a ceasefire just weeks after 7 October. Ed Miliband’s willingness to accurately describe Israel’s actions in the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” indicate a change in attitude that could lead to more concerted international action against Israel.
after newsletter promotion
In the US, support for Israel has fallen through the floor. For a Democrat who wants to be president in 2028 there is no credible path to the White House that doesn’t involve support for the Palestinian cause. And yet, we cannot simply close our eyes and hope that a change in America will magically restore the world to how it was on 6 October 2023.
N or should we pretend that the previous era was one we should wish to return to. Did we enter a new world on 7 October, or did we just notice where we were? In the three years before the Hamas attack, the wars in Tigray and Sudan saw many of the same trends play out.
In Tigray, the northernmost part of Ethiopia , a war between the central government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front killed 600,000 people. There were brutal massacres, forced starvation, widespread use of drones – and absolutely no accountability. In Sudan, too, hospitals have been hit by drones, women have been raped, children have been shot dead. Again, we could see it happen. Again, there were no consequences.
Gaza, though, has undoubtedly accelerated the trend, normalising the immoral. The wars that have begun, that have spiralled out of control and pulled more countries and more actors into their orbit, cannot easily be stopped. There is a momentum to this conflict, a hardening of positions, as each new outrage leads to a response. When there is impunity, when there is no price that those responsible will ever pay, there are terrifyingly few levers to pull. If war crimes go unpunished, they only escalate.
And so a family in Addis Ababa fears the sound of a drone crashing into their home. A village in Lebanon is evacuated, destroyed and the land made uninhabitable. A mundane job at Riyadh airport becomes a daily deadly gamble . A crew of badly paid seafarers pray to their gods as they cross through the strait of Hormuz. The dreams of millions of children shrink from university, fame or fortune, to the brute reality of survival.
And in Gaza, crammed into tents, deprived

articles.title_orig: Flu season is already here. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu shots.
articles.title_zh: Flu season is already here. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu shots.
articles.content_orig:
Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?
Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where one of this season's two influenza deaths so far has occurred, according to authorities.
The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.
"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.
"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."
Doctors say flu season is ahead of schedule this year as cases pop up across Ontario
1 dead, more than 400 confirmed flu cases ahead of vaccine availability in Alberta
But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.
Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.
According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Oct. 3, there have been 3,315 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August. More than 1,140 of those cases were detected in the most recent week of available data, showing that cases are picking up.
Influenza has been associated with two deaths so far this flu season, national figures state. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 age range, authorities say. Authorities haven't yet shared where the second death occurred.
It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 3, 4.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.6 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.
But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. Other areas seeing cases creep up include Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Alberta.
"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.
B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign
He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.
"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on."
Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.
In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.
You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year
"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.
"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."
Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.
The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.
This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.
Nova Scotia opens COVID-19, flu vaccine bookings ahead of respiratory illness season
Flu and COVID-19 vaccinations underway in B.C. as respiratory illness season arrives early
Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school
He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.
It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.
About 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)
Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 4.1 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.5 per cent at the same time in 2025.
The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.
Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.
New Brunswick , Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.
Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.
In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, including seniors aged 65 and up, hospitalized patients, long-term care residents and health-care workers, according to the provincial government. They don't open to the general public until Oct. 26 .
In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20 . It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.
Updated COVID-19, flu vaccines available in N.B. on Oct. 13
Alberta now providing free RSV antibodies to newborns after calls from pediatricians to expand access
Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta , with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.
In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.
COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.
Before heading out to the pharmacy or clinic, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure you're eligible and that providers near you have received the necessary supplies to offer shots and aren't experiencing delays.

articles.title_orig: India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders detained; New Delhi in lockdown
articles.title_zh: India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders detained; New Delhi in lockdown
articles.content_orig:
India coackroach Janta party protest: Party leader arrested as thousands of police deployed
Police in India’s capital New Delhi have detained more than 1,000 protesters, opposition politicians, journalists, student union leaders, lawyers and the founders of the “Cockroach” youth movement in an effort to quash their demonstration demanding the resignation of the election chief.
The satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other youth groups had announced a protest in the subcontinent’s capital for Saturday, aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
The protesters accuse the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of using the SIR to sway election results, ‌in collusion with its appointees in the election commission, including Kumar.
Meanwhile, opposition parties say the voter deletions also affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP, and have cast a shadow on elections in the world’s largest democracy.
The CJP had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in central Delhi.
But on Saturday, the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.
The Indian capital was also in lockdown with thousands of police and paramilitary personnel deployed across the city, trains to New Delhi cancelled, mobile internet services suspended and metro stations and markets shuttered, in an effort to stop the protests.
BJP spokesman Sambit Patra has dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchic elements”.
“Their flop show has been completely demolished,” Patra said. “What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India’s story. India is calm and going ahead under good governance,” he told reporters.
Police detained the founder of ⁠the CJP Abhijeet Dipke, as well as his associates Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, in an aeroplane upon arrival at New Delhi from Mumbai.
Dipke shared a video on his Instagram channel, showing a team of police officers entering the Air India plane after it landed. As they came closer, he said: “I have come to get arrested. I am not afraid of you guys.”
In another video shared by Ranka, Dipke was seen addressing the other passengers on the flight.
“It was nice to know you all. We can see where the nation is heading,” he said. “This is dictatorship where Delhi police has entered in the flight and trying to arrest us.”
Delhi police also detained other CJP members, YouTuber and Modi critic Dhruv Rathee , Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a leftist group affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist), Dipankar Bhattacharya, the general secretary of the party,  Prashant Bhushan, a senior lawyer at the Supreme Court, politicians Yogendra Yadav and Mamata Banerjee, among others.
Despite the detentions of the founders of the youth movement, small protests took place elsewhere in the city, including at the popular crafts market “Dilli Haat”.
But journalists trying to cover these protests and people attempting to protest anywhere in the capital were also detained and whisked away in police buses.
Shranaya, a state committee member of the left-wing Students’ Federation of India (SFI), who goes by her first name, told Al Jazeera that their office in New Delhi had been under surveillance for hours, but members inside had managed to escape and protest.
“This is dictatorship live and in front of us, just to protect a bureaucrat who steals elections for the BJP on Modi’s behest. They are murdering democracy in the daylight in the Indian capital,” she said.
“This government is unaware of the power of the people, and that is our upper hand. We do not have weapons, but we have zeal. We will be again on the streets, and we will keep returning,” she added. “We are students. We are unemployed. We are ‘cockroaches’ – and we will return.”
She then climbed a barricade but was dragged away by police and taken away in a bus.
The opposition Congress party’s president, Mallikarjun Kharge slammed Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government after the detentions.
“Modi government has turned the ‘Mother of Democracy’ into a ‘Muzzled Democracy’!” he posted on X. “Detentions, arrests, jails, lathis [batons] and pellets cannot deter the people of India. Since the days of our freedom struggle, the youth have been at the forefront of shaping the nation’s destiny,” he added.
Global human rights group Amnesty International warned that the detentions signal the Indian government’s desperate attempts to “supress critical voices”.
“The authorities must immediately and unconditionally release all those who have been detained solely for exercising their right to Freedom of Expression and Right to peaceful assembly,” Aakar Patel, chair of board of Amnesty International India, told Al Jazeera.
The Committee to Protect Journalists urged Indian police to “respect journalists”.
“We call on the Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in Delhi and the police response without interference,” Kunal Majumder, CPJ’s Asia Pacific programme coordinator, told Al Jazeera.
The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls in advance of recent state polls.
The unrest is also coming before a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.
Sanjay Kapoor, editor of Hard News Magazine and a political analyst, told Al Jazeera that it is “very strange” to see Modi’s government “so panic-driven and fearful of what the protesters might do”.
“The truth is that the BJP and the centre have been very, very scared of how it will all play out,” he said.
Kapoor noted that most of the people coming to the protests do not want Modi’s BJP to continue to govern.
“Modi’s government has begun to lose a lot of credibility at the moment,” he said. “BJP is afraid that the ground has shifted dramatically against them and they would find it very difficult to come back to power,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Tree rips through roof of Crestview family home during Hurricane Isaias
articles.title_zh: Tree rips through roof of Crestview family home during Hurricane Isaias
articles.content_orig:
CRESTVIEW, Fla. -- For one Crestview family, Hurricane Isaias hit harder than expected.
For Ashley Weeks and her family, the devastation is personal. A tree from their backyard split on top of their house, gutting their roof and bringing stormwater inside.
The owner says they are from the area, but have only lived in this home for two years. Destruction from Hurricane Isaias stretched more than 30 miles inland from the coast.
"Just scary, everything, my whole life is in the house," Weeks said. "We heard a loud like something, like a bomb went off in the house. It was so loud. And I got up and went and seen the tree through the roof and it was freaking out."
The tree landed on the roof near her daughter's bedroom. What was once their ceiling is now just piles of wet debris in their living room and kitchen.
Weeks  says she, Brian Johnson, her daughter, their four dogs, and a reptile were all inside the house at the time of the crash. Everyone made it out alive.
"I don't think anybody else would be good who experiences something like this," said Johnson. "But you never think it's gonna happen to you until it does."
Weeks says her family has called this house their home for the last two years. There's certain memories in the home she wanted to preserve.
"My daughter's father passed away a few years ago," Weeks said. "Her necklace with his ashes was in that house, and she was upset we came back at that like our pictures stuff that matters the most to us.
Outside the home, a second tree  collapsed in their front yard. The family is still processing the devastation, but are forced to think about next steps.
Weeks says the family spent the night at her fathers house. Her next steps are to figure out how to restore her home.

Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Two Philadelphia police officers were shot early Saturday while responding to a report of an armed man in the western part of the city.
One officer, a 40-year-old who has two children, was shot three times, Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel said during a news conference.
The other officer, a 33-year-old who has five children, was shot 12 times, Bethel said.
Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel, seen on May 8, 2025, gave an update on the officers who were shot while responding to a call in the western part of the city on Oct. 10, 2026. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"I am so damn proud of the men and women who serve in this department. Consistently, they go into danger, and they give their lives for this job," Bethel told reporters. "And so we ask for those prayers, and we ask for you to support our men and women out there, and what they give for this profession."
Just after 12:20 a.m., the officers were dispatched to 140 North 52nd Street following a report of a man with a gun on a porch, Bethel said.
About 30 minutes later, the officers arrived at the address and came under "significant gunfire" once they were on the porch.
Shortly after shots were fired, Bethel said additional officers and a SWAT team found the original responding officers on the porch with gunshot wounds.

The suspect fired at two additional officers, Bethel said, but the SWAT team was able to locate the man in a tree and take him into custody.
The officers who were shot were taken to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center for surgery. Their conditions are unknown.
The suspect reportedly ambushed the officers by running down an alley and shooting at them, local outlet WPVI reported.
FILE - The two Philadelphia police officers who were shot were taken to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center. (Al Bello/Getty Images)

The suspect, whose name has not yet been released, was found with two handguns and a shotgun, Bethel said. One of the handguns belonged to one of the officers who had been shot.
The Philadelphia Police Department did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title_orig: IsDB Group Chairman leads delegation at the 2026 World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok
articles.title_zh: IsDB Group Chairman leads delegation at the 2026 World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok
articles.content_orig:
Jeddah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, 10 October 2026 - H.E. Dr. Muhammad Al Jasser, Chairman of the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) Group, will lead a high-level delegation to the 2026 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group (WBG) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), taking place in Bangkok, Thailand, from 12 to 19 October 2026.
Amidst a complex global economic landscape, Dr. Al Jasser will engage in strategic dialogues with finance ministers, leaders of multilateral development banks, and key international partners. The discussions will primarily focus on economic stability, trade resilience, scaling development finance, and deepening regional cooperation.
Dr. Al Jasser will hold a bilateral meeting with H.E. Mr. Ekniti Nitithanprapas, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance of Thailand, the host country.
On Wednesday, 14 October, he will feature as a panelist for the session, “Trade Diversification in Turbulent Times: Implications for Economic Stability and Growth.” The discussion will address how shifting global trade dynamics impact economic resilience, focusing on strategies for trade diversification and economic transformation in emerging markets and developing economies, particularly IsDB member countries.
Dr. Al Jasser will also deliver a keynote address at the high-level forum, “Islamic Finance: From Crisis Resilience to Transition Finance,” highlighting the sector’s vital role in contemporary economic transitions.
Additionally, Dr. Al Jasser will participate in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan (MENAP) Ministers and Governors Meeting with the IMF Managing Director, as well as the Arab Governors Meeting with the WBG President.
On the sidelines of the Annual Meetings, Dr. Al Jasser will conduct bilateral meetings with IsDB Governors and senior representatives from leading international development institutions. Expected meetings include leadership from the WBG, the IMF, the French Development Agency (AFD), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD).
These engagements provide a critical platform for exchanging insights on shared priorities and building stronger global partnerships to drive sustainable economic development across IsDB member countries. For media inquiries, please contact: media@isdb.org

articles.title_orig: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
articles.title_zh: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
articles.content_orig:
Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets.
As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs.
In March, Dollar General said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ's Wholesale Club said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs . In September, Lululemon said it cut North America SKUs by 15%.
Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make.
When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don't end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems.
"If you have zero discounting, you're not taking enough fashion risk," said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. "But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly."
Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns.
Under Armour's operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue.
"Today, we're managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy," said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. "We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price."
Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power.
Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years.
"Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things," said Siegel. "Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer."
Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand.
Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level.
"It's a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception," said Siegel.
He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026.
Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is "rebalancing" its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June.
For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ's, cutting down the assortment doesn't necessarily give them the ability to raise prices.
Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business.
"When you shrink a box ... and say, I'm going to focus more on curation, you're getting smaller, but you're trying to reestablish why someone's walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn't necessarily help your bottom line as much," said Siegel.
BJ's CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren't previously offered.
"That is sourcing sales growth as well and sort of giving us the formula where we can cut SKUs, and see sales go up, and see margin dollars go up," Eddy said on the company's fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August.
In June 2025, Dollar General said the elimination of 1,000 SKUs from the previous year opened up more shelf space for its best-selling products and added to its top line. By March 2026, the company said, it had reduced up to 1,500 SKUs, providing benefits to the overall supply chain.
"Being more productive there means getting product to the shelf faster and being there for the consumer with the right amount of items and products that she's looking for as quickly as we possibly can," Dollar General CEO Todd Vasos said in the company's fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August. "As we go forward, the team is looking at continued SKU rationalization, albeit probably more surgical in nature."
Successfully slashing products from shelves is difficult in practice.
Box stores risk losing customers to competitors that offer the products they scrapped. BJ's, for instance, acknowledged that a previous attempt to cut SKUs was unsuccessful.
"We just cut SKUs which cut sales, and then we added some SKUs back and so really what we're doing now is removing unnecessary choice," Eddy said on the company's earnings call in August. "Think about in traditional soda, we don't carry cans and one-liters and two-liters of the same product anymore."
Meanwhile, publicly traded brands that acknowledge sales need to decline in order for the business to grow still have answers to investors in the near term.
"It's hard for a company ever to say we need to shrink anything, but it's dramatically harder to say we need to shrink revenues," said Siegel. "Frequently we find that brands hit a peak, a healthy peak, extend past the peak by forcing it and then find their way back down pretty harshly."
